q: Which of the following is used to compare means of two or more groups?
concept: The answer is a: analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used to compare the means of two or more groups. ANOVA was developed by Ronald A. Fisher in the 1920s, notably in Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925); George Snedecor later named its statistic F in Fisher's honour. It compares means by analysing variances. The total sum of squares is split into variation between the group means and variation within the groups (error). The F ratio is the between-groups mean square divided by the within-groups mean square: if the groups differ only by chance, F is close to 1; a large F means the group means differ more than chance allows. A significant F says that at least one mean differs, and post hoc tests such as Tukey's then locate the difference. ANOVA assumes a continuous dependent variable, independent observations, roughly normal distributions and equal variances. It is used for three or more means because running many t-tests would inflate the familywise Type I error rate, but it also works for two groups, where F = t squared and both tests give the same p-value. Example: a researcher compares anxiety scores after CBT, medication and a waiting list; a one-way ANOVA tests all three means in one step. Option a is right because only ANOVA handles both two and more than two group means. Exam trap: the t-test compares at most two means, so it fails the 'or more' part of the stem; chi-square compares frequencies, not means.

traps.b: The t-test, published by William Sealy Gosset under the pen name 'Student' (1908), compares the means of only two groups or conditions; it cannot handle three or more in a single test.
traps.c: Multiple regression predicts one continuous outcome from several predictor variables and estimates each predictor's unique contribution; it models relationships rather than being the standard test for comparing group means.
traps.d: Chi-square, introduced by Karl Pearson in 1900, compares observed and expected frequencies of categorical data, such as how many men and women chose each option; it does not compare means.

q: Which of the following is not an IQ test?
concept: The answer is c: IDEAS is not an IQ test. IDEAS is the Indian Disability Evaluation and Assessment Scale, published by the Indian Psychiatric Society (2002) to rate the disability caused by mental illness. It is used in India to certify psychiatric disability so that patients can receive government benefits. The clinician rates the person's functioning in four areas (self-care, interpersonal activities, communication and understanding, and work) and adds a score for the duration of illness; the total converts to a percentage of disability. It measures how much an illness limits daily life, not intelligence. The other three are intelligence tests. C. M. Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests of Intelligence (1955) has five subtests (Kohs Block Design, Alexander Pass-Along, Pattern Drawing, Immediate Memory and Picture Construction) and suits people with little schooling. The WAIS, by David Wechsler (1955), is the standard adult intelligence scale. MISIC is Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children, Arthur J. Malin's (1969) Indian adaptation of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children. For example, Arjun, who has had schizophrenia for six years, is assessed with IDEAS for a disability certificate, while his younger cousin with learning problems is tested with MISIC to obtain an IQ. Option c is right because IDEAS yields a disability percentage, not an IQ. Exam trap: the acronym looks as if it measures 'ideas' or thinking ability. Also do not confuse it with other Indian tools such as the Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA), which is not an IQ test either.

traps.a: The Bhatia battery (C. M. Bhatia, 1955) is an Indian performance test of intelligence with five subtests, giving a performance IQ without needing literacy.
traps.b: The WAIS (David Wechsler; fourth edition 2008) is the most widely used adult IQ test, giving a Full Scale IQ from four index scores.
traps.d: MISIC (Arthur J. Malin, 1969) is an Indian adaptation of the WISC that yields verbal, performance and full-scale IQs for children.

q: Which of the following therapies is not considered as a form of third wave therapies?
concept: The answer is d: classic behaviour therapy is the first wave, not a third-wave therapy. Steven Hayes (2004) described the history of behavioural and cognitive treatment as three waves. The first wave, behaviour therapy, took off in the 1950s and 1960s and applied learning principles directly to observable behaviour: systematic desensitisation by Joseph Wolpe (1958), exposure, and operant methods such as token economies built on the work of B. F. Skinner (1953). The second wave, cognitive therapy, added thoughts as targets in the 1960s and 1970s: Albert Ellis (1962) and Aaron Beck (1979) taught clients to identify and dispute irrational or distorted beliefs, and the merger of the two waves became CBT. The third wave, from the 1990s, changes the person's relationship to thoughts and feelings rather than their content, using mindfulness, acceptance, values and dialectics. Its members include acceptance and commitment therapy (Steven Hayes, 1999), dialectical behaviour therapy (Marsha Linehan, 1993), mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale, 2002) and other mindfulness-based interventions such as mindfulness-based stress reduction (Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979). Example: when Riya thinks "I am a failure", a second-wave therapist asks her to examine the evidence, while an ACT therapist asks her to notice it as just a thought and act on her values anyway. Option d is right because behaviour therapy is the original first wave, the base from which the later waves grew. Exam trap: DBT keeps "behaviour therapy" in its name, so students sometimes pick it, but it is a core third-wave therapy, while plain behaviour therapy is the one that does not belong.

traps.a: Dialectical behaviour therapy (Marsha Linehan, 1993), built for borderline personality disorder, balances acceptance and change through mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness; it is a core third-wave therapy despite its name.
traps.b: Mindfulness-based interventions such as MBSR (Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979) and MBCT (Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale, 2002) train non-judgemental, present-moment awareness and are central to the third wave.
traps.c: Acceptance and commitment therapy (Steven Hayes, 1999) uses acceptance, defusion and values-based action to build psychological flexibility; Hayes himself named the third wave, and ACT is its flagship.

q: Changes in consciousness are likely seen in:
concept: The answer is d: changes in consciousness are characteristically seen in delirium. Delirium is an acute brain failure. DSM-5-TR defines it as a disturbance of attention (difficulty directing, focusing, sustaining or shifting it) and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment) that develops over a short period, usually hours to a few days, fluctuates in severity during the day, and brings an additional cognitive change such as disorientation, memory loss or perceptual disturbance, with evidence of a physical cause. Older texts called this clouding of consciousness, the mildest lowering of awareness. Causes include infection, metabolic or electrolyte upset, hypoxia, drugs, intoxication or withdrawal (delirium tremens) and surgery. Typical features are visual hallucinations and illusions, a reversed sleep-wake cycle, worsening in the evening (sundowning) and diffuse slowing on the EEG. Subtypes are hyperactive, hypoactive (quiet and easily missed) and mixed. Example: an 80-year-old woman two days after hip surgery is lucid in the morning but at night is drowsy, cannot follow a conversation, thinks she is at home and picks at the bedclothes; a urinary infection is found, and she clears when it is treated. Option d is right because disturbed consciousness and attention, with acute onset and fluctuating course, is the defining feature of delirium. Exam trap: in schizophrenia, depression and early dementia consciousness is clear; the most reliable clue separating delirium from dementia is disturbed attention or consciousness with acute onset, not memory loss or hallucinations, which occur in both.

traps.b: Depression may impair concentration, but the sensorium is clear; even in depressive pseudodementia attention and consciousness are preserved.
traps.c: In dementia consciousness stays clear until the late stages, while memory and other cognitive losses progress over months to years; fluctuating attention in Lewy body dementia and delirium superimposed on dementia are well-known exceptions, not the rule.

q: A procedure that establishes a sequence of responses, which lead to a reward following the final response, by working backwards from the final response is called:
concept: The answer is c: building a sequence of responses by working backwards from the final, rewarded response is called chaining, here backward chaining. A behaviour chain is a series of responses in which each step produces the cue (discriminative stimulus) for the next, and only the last step earns the main reward. B. F. Skinner (1938), in The Behavior of Organisms, described how such chains hold together: each stimulus in the chain is both a conditioned reinforcer for the response before it and a signal for the response after it. In backward chaining the trainer first teaches the final link, which is followed at once by the reward; then adds the second-to-last link, whose completion leads into the already learned final step; and so on back to the first link. Because the learner always finishes with success and reward, the method suits young children and people with intellectual disability. Forward chaining starts from the first step instead, and total task presentation practises all the steps every time. Example: to teach Aarav, a child with autism, to tie his shoelaces, the therapist does every step except the final pull, lets Aarav complete it and praises him. Once that is easy, Aarav does the last two steps, then three, until he ties the whole lace himself. Option c is right because chaining links responses into a sequence, and the stem describes its backward form. Exam trap: shaping (a) also builds new behaviour step by step, but it reinforces successive approximations to a single target response, not a sequence of different responses linked together.

traps.a: Shaping (B. F. Skinner) reinforces successive approximations to one new target response, for example rewarding a rat for facing the lever, then touching it, then pressing it; it refines a single behaviour rather than linking a sequence backwards.
traps.b: Stimulus control is when a response occurs reliably in the presence of a particular discriminative stimulus and not in its absence (stopping at a red light); it concerns when a behaviour happens, not how a sequence is built.
traps.d: Stimulus generalisation is responding to stimuli similar to the trained one, as when Little Albert's conditioned fear of a white rat spread to other furry objects (John Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920); it is the spread of a response, not a training procedure.

q: According to Freud's structural model, which component of personality operates based on the reality principle?
concept: In the structural (tripartite) model of the mind proposed by Sigmund Freud, personality is divided into three agencies: the id, the ego, and the superego. The id is the primitive reservoir of instinctual drives and operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate discharge of tension regardless of consequences. The superego embodies internalized parental and societal standards, dividing into the conscience (which punishes with guilt) and the ego-ideal (which rewards with pride); it functions on a moral or idealistic principle. The ego is the executive of the personality and operates on the reality principle: it mediates between the demands of the id, the prohibitions of the superego, and the constraints of the external world, delaying gratification until a safe and appropriate object or moment is found. The ego relies on secondary-process thinking, which is logical and reality-oriented, in contrast to the id's irrational primary-process thinking. Because the reality principle is precisely the ego's mode of operation, option b is correct. Note that option d, the conscious mind, belongs to Freud's earlier topographic model, not the structural one.

traps.a: The id runs on the pleasure principle, demanding immediate gratification, not the reality principle.
traps.c: The superego operates on a moral or idealistic principle (conscience and ego-ideal), not the reality principle.
traps.d: The conscious mind is a level of awareness in the topographic model, not one of the three structural agencies.

q: Sympathetic nerves are projected from……

options.b: Cervical- Sacral sections of spinal cord
options.d: All the sections of the spinal cord

concept: The answer is c: sympathetic nerves arise from the thoracic and lumbar sections of the spinal cord. The autonomic nervous system has two main divisions. The sympathetic division prepares the body for action; Walter Cannon (1915) called its emergency role the fight-or-flight response: the heart races, pupils widen, airways open and blood shifts to the muscles. Its preganglionic cell bodies lie in the lateral grey horn of spinal segments T1 to L2 (some books say L3), so it is called the thoracolumbar outflow. Their short axons leave through the ventral roots and synapse mostly in the sympathetic chain, a row of ganglia beside the spine, from which long postganglionic fibres run to the organs. Some fibres go straight to the adrenal medulla, which releases adrenaline into the blood. The parasympathetic division (rest and digest) is the craniosacral outflow: cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X (the vagus carries most of it) plus sacral segments S2 to S4, with ganglia near or inside the organs. For example, when Rohan steps off a kerb and a bus horn blasts beside him, his pounding heart and dry mouth come from sympathetic fibres that leave the upper thoracic segments of his spinal cord. Option c is right because thoracic-lumbar is the textbook location of the sympathetic preganglionic neurons. Exam trap: option b sounds like the parasympathetic pattern but is garbled; the parasympathetic outflow is cranial-sacral (brainstem plus sacral cord), and 'cervical-sacral' matches neither division.

traps.a: The brain gives rise to the cranial nerves, and the cranial part of the autonomic outflow (nerves III, VII, IX and X) is parasympathetic, not sympathetic.
traps.b: Cervical-sacral is not an autonomic outflow; it garbles 'craniosacral', the parasympathetic pattern (brainstem plus S2 to S4). Cervical segments contain no sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
traps.d: The sympathetic chain extends up into the neck, but sympathetic preganglionic neurons sit only in segments T1 to L2; cervical and sacral segments have none, so 'all the sections' is wrong.

q: According to the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), which route of persuasion occurs when individuals are motivated and able to process a persuasive message carefully?
concept: The answer is b: in the elaboration likelihood model the central route is taken when people are both motivated and able to think carefully about a message. Richard Petty and John Cacioppo (1986) argued that persuasion depends on elaboration, the amount of careful thought a person gives to the arguments. When motivation is high (the issue matters personally, or the person enjoys thinking, called high need for cognition) and ability is high (enough time and knowledge, no distraction), people take the central route: they weigh the quality of the arguments, so strong arguments persuade and weak ones backfire. Attitudes formed this way last longer, resist counter-arguments and predict behaviour. When either motivation or ability is low, people take the peripheral route: they respond to cues such as an attractive or famous source, the sheer number of arguments or a catchy jingle, and the change is weaker and short-lived. For example, Meera, who is about to buy a laptop for her PhD work, studies battery and processor comparisons (central route), while her cousin Rohan, who is only browsing, is swayed by the cricketer in the advertisement (peripheral route). Option b is right because careful processing by a motivated and able person is the definition of the central route. Exam trap: heuristic and systematic are the two routes of Shelly Chaiken's (1980) heuristic-systematic model, a sister theory; the ELM's own terms are central and peripheral.

traps.a: The peripheral route is taken when motivation or ability is low, so people rely on surface cues (source attractiveness, number of arguments) rather than argument quality. It is the opposite of the condition in the stem.
traps.c: The heuristic route belongs to Shelly Chaiken's (1980) heuristic-systematic model, where simple rules such as 'experts are usually right' guide judgement. It is not an ELM route, and it matches low-effort processing, not careful thought.
traps.d: 'Dual-process' is the umbrella name for the family of theories (the ELM, the heuristic-systematic model) that propose two modes of processing. It names the type of model, not one of its routes.

q: Freud's stage of latency is corroborating with _____ stage of Erikson's psychosocial development.
concept: The answer is c: Freud's latency stage matches Erikson's industry versus inferiority. Sigmund Freud (1905), in Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality, described five psychosexual stages: oral (birth to about 1), anal (about 1 to 3), phallic (about 3 to 6), latency (about 6 to puberty) and genital (puberty onwards). In latency the sexual drive is quiet, and energy goes into school learning, skills, same-sex friendships and hobbies. Erik Erikson (1950), in Childhood and Society, kept Freud's timetable for childhood but asked what social task each age poses. His eight psychosocial crises are trust versus mistrust (oral), autonomy versus shame and doubt (anal), initiative versus guilt (phallic), industry versus inferiority (latency), identity versus role confusion (adolescence, Freud's genital stage), and then three adult stages Freud never described: intimacy versus isolation, generativity versus stagnation, and integrity versus despair. In industry versus inferiority (about 6 to 12 years) the child learns the tools of the culture at school; success with teachers and peers builds the virtue of competence, while repeated failure or harsh comparison leaves a sense of inferiority. Erikson even labelled this stage 'school age (latency)'. Example: nine-year-old Arjun spends evenings building model aeroplanes and learning to bowl; when his teacher praises his science project he feels capable, but if he is always compared with his topper cousin he may come to feel he is no good at anything. Option c is right because latency and industry versus inferiority cover the same years and the same focus on skills and schooling. Exam trap: count the stages carefully; initiative versus guilt matches the phallic (play age) stage, and identity versus role confusion matches Freud's genital stage, not latency.

traps.b: Identity versus role confusion (adolescence, about 12 to 18 years) parallels Freud's genital stage at puberty, not latency.
traps.d: Intimacy versus isolation (young adulthood) is one of Erik Erikson's own adult stages and has no counterpart in Freud's scheme.

q: To represent the relationship and spread between two continuous variables visually, which graph is most appropriate?
concept: The answer is a scatter plot because it is specifically designed to display the relationship and the spread between two continuous (quantitative) variables at once. In a scatter plot, one variable is placed on the horizontal x-axis and the other on the vertical y-axis, and each individual case or observation is plotted as a single point at its (x, y) coordinates. The resulting cloud of points reveals several things at a glance: the direction of the relationship (whether points trend upward for a positive relationship or downward for a negative one), the form of the relationship (linear or curved), the strength (how tightly the points cluster around a line versus how widely they scatter), and any outliers that fall away from the main pattern. This makes it the natural companion to the correlation coefficient and to regression analysis, both of which quantify what the scatter plot shows visually. The distractors each serve a different purpose worth knowing for the exam: a histogram shows the distribution shape of one continuous variable, a bar chart compares one variable across distinct categories, and an ogive plots cumulative frequency to read off percentiles and medians. Because the question asks about the relationship and spread between two continuous variables simultaneously, the scatter plot is uniquely suited and is the correct choice.

traps.a: A histogram displays the frequency distribution of a single continuous variable using adjacent bars, not the joint relationship between two variables.
traps.b: A bar chart compares values across discrete categories with separated bars; it is for categorical data, not the relationship between two continuous variables.
traps.d: An ogive is a cumulative frequency curve for one variable, showing how many cases fall below given values, not the association between two variables.

q: In WAIS-IV which of the following subtest belongs to the Perceptual Reasoning Index scale?
concept: The answer is b: Visual Puzzles is a core subtest of the WAIS-IV Perceptual Reasoning Index. The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, fourth edition (WAIS-IV, 2008), descends from David Wechsler's Wechsler-Bellevue scale (1939) and gives a Full Scale IQ plus four index scores. Verbal Comprehension measures verbal reasoning and knowledge (Similarities, Vocabulary, Information; Comprehension supplemental). Perceptual Reasoning measures non-verbal, visual-spatial reasoning: its core subtests are Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Visual Puzzles, with Figure Weights and Picture Completion supplemental. Working Memory measures holding and manipulating information in mind (Digit Span, Arithmetic; Letter-Number Sequencing supplemental). Processing Speed measures quick visual scanning and copying (Symbol Search, Coding; Cancellation supplemental). In Visual Puzzles the person looks at a completed design and must choose, within a time limit, the three pieces that together would make it, which means mentally rotating and fitting shapes without touching any blocks. For example, Aditi sees a square design and picks three of six fragments that would rebuild it; she is using spatial reasoning, not words or memory span. Visual Puzzles, Figure Weights and Cancellation were new subtests in the WAIS-IV. Option b is right because Visual Puzzles is one of the three core Perceptual Reasoning subtests. Exam trap: Digit Span and Letter-Number Sequencing feel like puzzles, but they belong to Working Memory, and Symbol Search, though visual, belongs to Processing Speed because it is scored for speed.

q: The aim of the ______ was to regulate training policies and programs in the field of disability rehabilitation and standardize training courses for professionals working with people with disabilities.
concept: The answer is b: the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) Act 1992 was passed to regulate and standardise the training of professionals who work with people with disabilities. The Rehabilitation Council of India began in 1986 as a registered society, and the RCI Act 1992 made it a statutory body (in force from 22 June 1993); the Act was amended in 2000. Its jobs are to regulate and monitor training policies and programmes in disability rehabilitation, to set minimum standards and standardise syllabi, to recognise institutions and qualifications, and to keep the Central Rehabilitation Register of qualified professionals. Practising without registration is an offence under the Act. The RCI sits under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not the Ministry of Health. Clinical psychologists, rehabilitation psychologists, special educators, audiologists and speech therapists all come under it, which is why an Indian clinical psychologist must hold an RCI-recognised qualification and be on the RCI register. For example, when Meera finishes her clinical psychology training and wants to practise, she applies for RCI registration; the Mental Healthcare Act then counts her as a mental health professional because of that qualification. Option b is right because the stem lists exactly the RCI Act's purposes: regulating training policies and programmes and standardising courses for rehabilitation professionals. Exam trap: the other three Acts are rights or care laws, not training laws. Examiners rely on the shared word 'disability' in the PwD and RPwD Acts to pull candidates away from the RCI Act, which is about the professionals, not the people they serve.

traps.d: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 is a rights-based mental health care law (right to access care, advance directives, decriminalising attempted suicide). It defines a clinical psychologist by an RCI-recognised qualification but does not regulate disability training.

q: The primary feature distinguishing bipolar I disorder from bipolar II disorder is:
concept: The answer is c: the presence of at least one manic episode is what distinguishes bipolar I disorder from bipolar II disorder. Emil Kraepelin grouped recurrent mood illness as manic-depressive insanity in 1899, and Karl Leonhard separated unipolar from bipolar forms in 1957. DSM-5-TR defines the episodes by severity and duration. A manic episode is at least one week of abnormally elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy (any duration if hospitalisation is needed), causing marked impairment, hospitalisation or psychotic features. A hypomanic episode has the same kinds of symptoms for at least four days but is not severe enough to cause marked impairment and has no psychosis. Bipolar I needs only one manic episode; depressions are common but not required. Bipolar II needs at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, and never a full manic episode; a first mania changes the diagnosis to bipolar I. Example: a woman with two past depressions has a four-day spell of little sleep, extra productivity and chattiness that friends notice but that does not disrupt her job: bipolar II. If she later spends her savings, believes God has chosen her and is admitted to hospital, the diagnosis becomes bipolar I. Option c is right because mania is required for bipolar I and excluded from bipolar II. Exam trap: bipolar II is not simply milder bipolar I, since its depressions are frequent and disabling, and hypomania can occur in both types, so hypomania alone does not separate them.

traps.d: Absence of mood symptoms describes neither disorder; both are defined by episodes of mood disturbance.

q: Hope, happiness, optimism and flow takes together as
concept: The answer is b: hope, happiness, optimism and flow are studied together as positive psychology. Positive psychology is the scientific study of what makes life go well: positive emotions, strengths of character, and the conditions that let people and communities flourish. Martin Seligman launched it in his 1998 presidential address to the American Psychological Association, arguing that psychology had spent decades on illness and damage and too little on well-being; with Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi he set out its aims in a special issue of the American Psychologist (2000). Each word in the stem is one of its signature topics. Hope theory (C. R. Snyder, 1991) sees hope as goal-directed willpower plus waypower, the ability to find paths to goals. Happiness, studied as subjective well-being by Ed Diener (1984), is life satisfaction with frequent positive and rare negative feelings. Learned optimism (Martin Seligman, 1990) is a habit of explaining bad events as temporary and specific rather than permanent and pervasive. Flow (Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, 1990) is total absorption in a task whose challenge matches one's skill. Example: when Meera loses all sense of time while practising the sitar, she is in flow, a state that positive psychologists measure and try to increase. Option b is right because hope, happiness, optimism and flow form the core research cluster of positive psychology. Exam trap: humanistic psychology (Abraham Maslow, 1954; Carl Rogers, 1951) also stresses growth and the good life and is a forerunner, but it relied mostly on theory and case study; the research movement that grouped these four topics is positive psychology.

q: The idea that personality can be created by the interaction between a person, his environment and his behaviour is known as:
concept: The answer is c: the idea that personality grows out of the mutual influence of the person, the environment and behaviour is Albert Bandura's reciprocal determinism. Albert Bandura (1978), in 'The self system in reciprocal determinism', argued against two one-way views: the radical behaviourism of B. F. Skinner (1953), in which the environment shapes behaviour, and trait views, in which inner dispositions drive behaviour. In his model, later called triadic reciprocal causation in Social Foundations of Thought and Action (1986), three sets of factors are joined by two-way arrows: person factors (thoughts, expectations, self-efficacy, feelings), behaviour, and the environment (other people, rewards, settings). Each is both cause and effect. People are not simply pushed by their surroundings; their behaviour also selects and changes the environment they then meet. Example: Meera expects to do badly in statistics (person), so she skips practice (behaviour); her teacher, seeing little effort, gives her less attention (environment), which lowers her expectation further. If she joins a study group, the same loop can run the other way. Option c is right because reciprocal determinism is the exact name for this three-way, mutual influence. Exam trap: interactionism also says that person and situation work together, but it is a two-factor model in which behaviour is only the outcome; Bandura's addition is that behaviour is itself a third, active cause.

traps.a: Circular creation is not a term in personality theory; it borrows the circular feel of the model but names no theory.
traps.b: Interactionism comes from the person-situation debate that followed Walter Mischel's (1968) critique of traits, as in Norman Endler and David Magnusson's (1976) interactional psychology: in its usual form, behaviour is the product of person x situation rather than a third cause that changes the other two.
traps.d: Combination theory is not an established personality theory; it is a made-up label that echoes the idea of combining factors.

q: What is the key brain structure that is often damaged in patients with anterograde amnesia?
concept: The correct answer is the hippocampus. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new long-term memories after the onset of brain damage, so the person cannot lay down new declarative (explicit) memories of events and facts, even though memories formed before the injury and immediate short-term memory may be relatively intact. The key brain structure involved is the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure in the medial temporal lobe that is essential for consolidating new experiences from short-term into long-term memory. The most famous case in all of neuropsychology is patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), who had large portions of his medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, surgically removed in 1953 to treat severe epilepsy. Afterwards he was left with a profound, permanent anterograde amnesia: he could hold a conversation but would forget it minutes later and never formed new memories of the people he met daily. Crucially, H.M. could still learn new motor skills (procedural memory) without remembering having practised them, which revealed that the hippocampus is critical for declarative memory but not for procedural memory. This dissociation established the hippocampus as the central structure for forming new conscious memories, making it the correct answer.

traps.b: The cerebral cortex stores consolidated long-term memories across its association areas, but it is the hippocampus, not the cortex, whose damage prevents forming new memories.
traps.c: The amygdala processes emotion and the emotional significance of memories, particularly fear, but does not itself cause anterograde amnesia.
traps.d: The hypothalamus regulates homeostatic drives such as hunger, thirst, and temperature, not the formation of new declarative memories.

q: In a study on conformity, participants often agreed with a clearly incorrect majority. Which of the following best explains this behavior?
concept: The answer is b: when participants agree with a clearly incorrect majority, the best explanation is normative social influence, conforming in order to be liked and accepted and to avoid rejection. Morton Deutsch and Harold Gerard (1955) separated two reasons for conformity. Informational social influence is conforming because we think others know better, so we privately accept their view; it is strongest when the situation is ambiguous. Normative social influence is going along with the group to fit in, often while privately disagreeing (public compliance). Solomon Asch (1951, 1956) showed this with a line judgement task. A real participant sat with a group of confederates, and on critical trials every confederate gave the same obviously wrong answer about which of three lines matched a standard line. Alone, people made almost no errors, yet with the group about 75 per cent conformed at least once, and about a third of all critical answers were wrong. Afterwards many said they knew the answer was wrong but did not want to stand out. When a single ally gave the right answer, conformity fell sharply. Example: in a college quiz team, Riya knows the answer is Delhi, but when all four teammates confidently say Mumbai, she nods along to avoid looking foolish. Option b is right because the answer was clearly wrong, so the group offered no useful information; the pressure came from the wish to be accepted. Exam trap: informational influence (a) is the near miss; it belongs to Muzafer Sherif's (1935) autokinetic study, where a still point of light in a dark room seemed to move, so people had no clear answer and used the group as a source of information.

traps.a: Informational social influence is conforming because others seem to know better, as in Muzafer Sherif's autokinetic study; with an obviously wrong answer, the group offers no real information.
traps.c: Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) is the tension of holding inconsistent cognitions, reduced by changing attitudes; it explains attitude change after behaviour, not yielding to a majority.
traps.d: Groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972) is faulty decision making in a cohesive group that values agreement over critical thinking, as in the Bay of Pigs invasion; it concerns group decisions, not one person yielding in a perception task.

q: Separation anxiety is a part of:
concept: The answer is b: separation anxiety appears in Bowlby's clear-cut attachment phase. John Bowlby (1969), in Attachment and Loss, argued that attachment is an evolved system that keeps a helpless infant close to a caregiver, and that it unfolds in four phases. In pre-attachment (birth to about 6 weeks) built-in signals such as crying, grasping, gazing and smiling bring any adult near, and the baby does not mind being left with a stranger. In attachment-in-the-making (6 weeks to 6 to 8 months) the infant responds differently to familiar people, smiling and babbling more for the mother, but still does not protest when she leaves. In clear-cut attachment (6 to 8 months to 18 months to 2 years) the baby has a definite attachment figure, uses her as a secure base for exploring, follows her once he can crawl, and shows separation anxiety (crying and protest when she leaves) and wariness of strangers. In formation of a reciprocal relationship (18 months to 2 years onwards) language and an understanding of the parent's plans let the child negotiate, so protest falls; Bowlby called this the goal-corrected partnership. Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson (1964), following Glasgow infants at home, found similar timing: specific attachments at about 7 months, with fear of strangers about a month later. Example: nine-month-old Kabir happily went to any relative at four months, but now screams whenever his mother leaves the room and clings to her when a visitor arrives. Option b is right because separation protest is the marker of the clear-cut phase. Exam trap: attachment-in-the-making sounds as if attachment is already in place, but the baby only prefers familiar people then; protest at separation and stranger wariness belong to clear-cut attachment.

q: Which biostatistical method is most appropriate to study relationships between two continuous psychological variables like stress level and sleep duration?
concept: Choosing a statistical test depends on the measurement level of the variables. Here both stress level and sleep duration are continuous variables, and the question asks about the relationship between them. The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, developed by Karl Pearson building on the work of Francis Galton, measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables, yielding a value r between minus one and plus one. It is the standard tool when the goal is to quantify how two interval or ratio variables covary. The distractors suit different data: the chi-square test, associated with Karl Pearson as well, tests associations between categorical variables using frequency counts; analysis of variance (ANOVA), developed by Ronald Fisher, compares the means of a continuous outcome across two or more groups defined by categorical predictors; and logistic regression models the probability of a categorical, usually binary, outcome. Because Pearson correlation is designed precisely to assess the relationship between two continuous variables, option c is correct.

traps.a: The chi-square test is for categorical (nominal) data, not two continuous variables.
traps.b: ANOVA compares means across groups defined by a categorical independent variable, not the relationship between two continuous variables.
traps.d: Logistic regression predicts a categorical (typically binary) outcome, so it does not model the association between two continuous variables directly.

q: Which type of psychological test measures personality traits, emotions, and attitudes?
concept: Psychological tests are grouped by what they measure. Personality tests are designed specifically to assess an individual's characteristic patterns of traits, emotions, attitudes, motives, and behavior. They fall into two broad families: objective (self-report) inventories such as the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), developed by Starke Hathaway and J. C. McKinley, and the 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire of Raymond Cattell, which use structured items scored against norms; and projective tests such as the Rorschach Inkblot Test of Hermann Rorschach and the Thematic Apperception Test of Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan, which present ambiguous stimuli to elicit unconscious material. The distractors measure different domains: achievement tests measure knowledge already acquired in academic areas, aptitude tests measure the potential to learn or perform future tasks, and neuropsychological tests assess brain-behavior relationships and cognitive functioning after injury or disease. Because personality tests are the category defined by measuring personality traits, emotions, and attitudes, option b is correct.

traps.a: Achievement tests measure acquired knowledge and skills in specific subject areas, not personality.
traps.c: Aptitude tests measure potential to learn or succeed at future tasks, not personality traits.
traps.d: Neuropsychological tests assess brain-behavior relationships and cognitive functioning, not personality traits per se.

q: Helping someone with a 'severe disorder' of functionality, personality, and aberrations of thoughts, feelings and behaviour is known as:
concept: The answer is b: helping someone with a severe disorder of functioning and personality, with marked disturbance of thoughts, feelings and behaviour, is psychotherapy. Psychotherapy is a planned, professional treatment in which a trained therapist uses psychological methods to relieve symptoms, change disturbed patterns of behaviour and promote personality growth, much as Lewis Wolberg (1954) defined it. It is used for clinical conditions such as major depression, personality disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorder. It often goes deeper and lasts longer, and it may aim to change long-standing personality patterns. Counselling, in the classic textbook contrast, serves essentially normal people facing developmental, situational or adjustment problems: choosing a career, exam stress, a break-up. It is usually shorter, focused on the present and on conscious problems, and draws on the person's existing strengths. For example, Meera, who is anxious about her board exams, is well served by a few counselling sessions. Arjun, who has had severe mood swings, self-harm and unstable relationships since his teens, needs psychotherapy. Option b is right because the stem stresses severity, personality-level problems and disturbed thoughts, feelings and behaviour, which are the province of psychotherapy. Exam trap: the line between the two is blurred in practice, and Carl Rogers (1942) used the words almost interchangeably in Counseling and Psychotherapy; but in exams, normal problems map to counselling and severe disorders to psychotherapy.

traps.c: Advising means giving information or recommendations about what to do; it involves no treatment of disturbed thoughts or feelings.
traps.d: Guiding (guidance), rooted in Frank Parsons's (1909) vocational guidance, helps people make educational and career choices; it is not treatment of severe disorders.

q: Waxy flexibility is:
concept: The answer is c: waxy flexibility is a disorder of motor behaviour. It is the English name for the Latin cerea flexibilitas. When the examiner moves the patient's arm, there is a slight, even resistance, like bending a soft wax candle, and the limb then stays in whatever position it has been placed, sometimes for minutes or hours. It is a sign of catatonia, the syndrome of disturbed movement first described by Karl Kahlbaum (1874). DSM-5 (2013) lists 12 catatonic signs and needs 3 or more: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia and echopraxia. Catatonia is a specifier that can attach to schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder and medical conditions, and it usually responds to lorazepam or electroconvulsive therapy. Catalepsy is holding a passively induced posture against gravity; waxy flexibility adds the feel of that slight resistance as the limb is moved. Example: Arjun, 24, admitted with catatonic schizophrenia, sits motionless; when the doctor raises his arm above his head and lets go, it stays there for ten minutes. Option c is right because waxy flexibility concerns posture and movement, so descriptive psychopathology files it under disorders of motor behaviour. Exam trap: catalepsy and cataplexy look alike. Cataplexy is a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter or strong emotion, in narcolepsy, with full consciousness; catalepsy, with its waxy flexibility, belongs to catatonia.

traps.a: Disorders of memory include amnesia, confabulation and paramnesias such as deja vu; a patient with waxy flexibility shows no change in memory.
traps.b: Disorders of emotion include blunted, flat or inappropriate affect, lability and anhedonia; waxy flexibility describes how the limbs respond to being moved, not how the person feels.
traps.d: Disorders of consciousness include clouding, delirium and coma; although stupor is one of the catatonic signs, a catatonic patient is usually alert, and many can later recall what went on around them.

q: The relative apparent motion of objects in the visual field as the viewer moves the head is called:
concept: The answer is c: the relative apparent motion of objects in the visual field as the viewer moves the head is called motion parallax. When you move, objects at different distances seem to move at different speeds and in different directions across your view. Near objects sweep past quickly in the direction opposite to your movement, while far objects move slowly and seem to travel with you. The brain reads these speed differences as distance: the faster something slides across the retina, the nearer it is. James J. Gibson (1950), in The Perception of the Visual World, widened the idea into optic flow, the whole pattern of motion that streams across the eyes as we move, which guides walking, driving and landing an aircraft. Motion parallax is a monocular depth cue, since it works with one eye, and a kinetic cue, since it needs movement. It sits beside the other monocular cues (linear perspective, relative size, interposition, texture gradient, aerial perspective and accommodation) and the two binocular cues (retinal disparity and convergence). The classic example: Arjun looks out of a train window and sees the electric poles beside the track flash backwards, while distant hills and the moon seem to glide along with the train. Option c is right because motion parallax is the name for the depth information carried by the different apparent motions of near and far objects when the head moves. Exam trap: accommodation is also a monocular depth cue, so it sounds plausible, but it comes from the lens changing shape to focus, not from movement.

traps.a: The image-retina system is the term of Richard Gregory (1966, Eye and Brain) for one way we detect movement, when an image runs across a still retina; it explains seeing motion, not the depth cue created by moving the head.
traps.b: Accommodation is the change in the lens's shape, made by the ciliary muscles, to focus on near or far objects; it is a monocular depth cue that works without any head movement and only at short distances.
traps.d: None of the above is wrong because motion parallax, option c, is the exact name for this cue.

q: The concept of the 'animus' archetype, given by Carl Jung, refers to:

options.a: The masculine side of a female psyche.
options.b: The repressed animalistic part of the mind.
options.c: The feminine side of a male psyche.
options.d: The repressed unpleasant thoughts and memories.

concept: The answer is a: in the theory of Carl Jung (1928), the animus is the masculine side of a woman's psyche. Carl Jung divided the unconscious into a personal unconscious, made of forgotten and repressed experiences organised into complexes, and a collective unconscious, inherited by all humans and filled with archetypes: universal patterns or images shaped by the shared experience of our ancestors. Four archetypes are developed most fully. The persona is the social mask. The shadow is the dark, primitive, animal side that we disown. The self is the archetype of wholeness, symbolised by the mandala. The anima and animus carry the other sex within each person: the anima is the feminine side of a man, and the animus is the masculine side of a woman. They come from humanity's long experience of the other sex, and they help explain attraction, since we project our anima or animus onto a partner who seems to match the inner image. Individuation, the lifelong move towards wholeness, needs these sides to be accepted rather than denied. Example: Meera, a gentle and accommodating teacher, discovers a firm, logical and assertive voice when she leads a staff meeting; a Jungian would call this her animus coming into awareness. Option a is right because animus is the term for the masculine element in the female psyche. Exam trap: the pair is easy to reverse (option c describes the anima), and 'animus' sounds like 'animal', which pulls students to option b, a description of the shadow. Memory aid: Latin -us endings are masculine (animus), and -a endings are feminine (anima).

traps.b: The repressed, animal-like side of the mind is the shadow, Carl Jung's archetype of the primitive and socially unacceptable impulses we disown; 'animus' only sounds like 'animal'.
traps.c: The feminine side of a man's psyche is the anima, the partner archetype of the animus; this option reverses the pair.
traps.d: Repressed unpleasant thoughts and memories make up Carl Jung's personal unconscious, organised into complexes (close to Sigmund Freud's repressed unconscious); they are personal, not an inherited archetype.

q: Which neurotransmitter is primarily associated with the reward system and addictive behaviors?
concept: The answer is b: dopamine is the neurotransmitter most closely tied to the brain's reward system and to addictive behaviour. The core reward circuit is the mesolimbic dopamine pathway: dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) of the midbrain send their axons to the nucleus accumbens in the ventral striatum, with links to the prefrontal cortex. James Olds and Peter Milner (1954) found that rats would press a lever again and again to receive electrical stimulation of this system, the first evidence for 'pleasure centres'. Natural rewards such as food, sex and social contact release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, and almost all addictive drugs raise it, directly or indirectly: cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, amphetamine releases it, and nicotine, alcohol and opioids increase the firing of dopamine neurons. Wolfram Schultz (1997) showed that dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error, firing more when a reward is better than expected, which teaches the brain what to seek. Repeated drug use changes this system so that drug cues trigger intense craving ('wanting'), the incentive-sensitisation theory of Terry Robinson and Kent Berridge (1993). Example: Arjun's phone pings with a new like on his post; the unpredictable reward triggers a dopamine burst, and he checks the phone again and again. Option b is right because dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway is the common final path of natural reward and drug addiction. Exam trap: serotonin (a) is the usual near miss because it is famous for mood and depression; it modulates mood and impulse control, but reward and craving belong to dopamine.

traps.a: Serotonin (5-HT), made in the raphe nuclei, regulates mood, sleep, appetite and impulse control and is the target of SSRIs for depression; it is not the main reward chemical.
traps.c: GABA is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter, enhanced by alcohol and benzodiazepines to calm neural activity; some drugs act on it, but the reward signal itself is dopamine.
traps.d: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, central to learning and long-term potentiation; it supports drug-related learning but is not the classic reward transmitter.
